newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU officials head west for U.S. air talks opener.
newsitem.headline: EU officials head west for U.S. air talks opener.

text.p: Officials from the European Commission, most of the 15 EU countries and representatives from Europe's airlines will converge on Washington next week for getting-to-know-you open skies talks with U.S. counterparts.

While the two-day meeting from Wednesday will be no more than "preliminary" according to European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock, it will set the scene for EU/U.S. aviation relations at a time rapid change in the transatlantic market.

"The first meeting will be largely procedural. We are interested to hear what the Commission's mandate is, how far it can go. We have not put anything on the table," a U.S. official told Reuters last week.

Talks are to cover so-called soft rights -- slot allocation, ground-handling rules, competition policy, code sharing and computer reservation systems -- leaving touchier issues like airline ownership rules and traffic rights for later.
"You cannot get very far on the issues which are of most interest to the Commission and member states without talking about the underlying issue of traffic rights," he said.
"They obviously cannot put rights on the table and without that, it's not a negotiation," the official added.
Rumbling in the background to the meeting will be looming open skies talks between the United States and Britain, upcoming U.S./France talks and the prospect of future talks with Spain.

Eventual deals with these three, while in no way a certainty, would sew up most of the north Atlantic market for U.S. carriers when combined with those already agreed between the United States and Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

"It's hard to know what would be left if we make significant progress with France or Spain. It may well be that we are in a race with the Commission to nail down as many of these things before having to discuss (U.S.) cabotage and ownership rights.
"I don't think we will have much interest in changing our ownership rules until we discuss traffic rights and even then, I don't know how keen we would be to change those rules," he said.

European Union rules allow foreign interests to hold up to 49 percent of an EU carrier, provided that control remains within the bloc. U.S. law limits foreign ownership to 25 percent of an airline's voting stock, again with control in U.S. hands.
Kinnock denied that bilateral deals would make talks pointless, leaving little to excite Washington in what remained.

"Ultimately there's got to be some kind of parity of legal and commercial standards between the two sides. Our market will grow and so it's commercially attractive. To have full and effective access to that market there's an entry fee," he said.

"It's not too late in all these developments, it's early days. It's early days for most of the European bilateral partnerships because the access which some of the airlines have to the USA is, if I were to say marginal it would be an exaggeration, whereas the access the other way is significant. That's a balance which ultimately is unsustainable," he said.
